title: Batch on one machine: pipes, sorting and hashing
goal: By the end, you can read a one-line shell pipeline as a batch job, choose between a hash map and a sort from the number of different keys, and work out how many runs and merge passes a sort needs.
opening:
Picture the evening after a school election. The ballots lie on a table, one name on each. You draw a tally sheet, a line per candidate, and make a mark per ballot. With five candidates the sheet fits on a postcard.

Now count something bigger: how often each library card in town was used this year. The sheet needs a line per card, and long before the end it fits on no table.

The tally is obvious and fast, so smart people try it first, and it passes every small test. It fails only when the names outgrow the room, and then all at once.

The last lesson, Why big data systems exist, priced a batch job by the bytes it reads, and left open what the job does with them. In this lesson, we'll answer a question about a log with five small programs and count it with a tally until memory runs out. Then we'll sort a file far bigger than the memory we allow. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: A 500 GB log holds about 2 billion different idempotency keys, unique labels that an app sends with its requests. Your laptop has 16 GB of memory and a 1 TB disk. Which way of counting the lines for each key can finish?
options: A Kotlin `HashMap` from key to count, a tally kept in memory, if you give the program 15 GB of memory
`sort | uniq -c`, two small programs that sort the keys and then count each run of equal ones
Neither: anything bigger than memory needs many computers
warmup.why: A hash map, the tally, must hold every different key until the end: 2 billion entries at about 100 bytes each is around 200 GB, far more than 15 GB. A sort only needs room for one chunk at a time. It sorts chunks that fit, writes each one to disk as a sorted piece called a run, and merges the runs while holding just a few lines. It needs disk space for the runs and gets slower as the input grows, but it doesn't run out of memory. Bigger than memory isn't where you need many computers. Bigger than one machine's disks, or its deadline, is.

sections.h: Five small programs answer a question about a log
sections.body:
A small company runs the program that records card payments for coffee shops, bookshops and grocers. Like most programs that answer requests over the web, it keeps a log. It sits behind NGINX, a free web server: the program that receives each request from the internet and passes it on. NGINX writes one line per request to a file called an access log. Here's one, in NGINX's usual format:

```text
10.0.22.243 - - [07/Nov/2026:00:00:00 +0000] "POST /v1/authorizations HTTP/1.1" 201 776 "-" "acquirer-sdk/4.2"
```

It holds the address of the computer that sent the request, the time and the request itself. Then come a status code (`201` means "created"), the size of the answer in bytes, and the name of the program that asked. The request's path, `/v1/authorizations`, is the address inside the payments program; this one asks for a card payment to be approved.

Someone at the company wants the five paths that got the most requests yesterday. The log has 2,000,000 lines, 231 MB: too much to read by eye, and far too little to need a cluster. One line typed into a shell (the program in a terminal window that runs the commands you type) answers it:

```bash
awk '{print $7}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -5
```

Read it left to right. `awk` is a small language for picking fields out of lines: `'{print $7}'` splits each line on blanks and prints the seventh field, the path. `sort` puts the paths in order. `uniq -c` turns each run of equal lines into one line with a count in front. `sort -rn` orders those lines by the count, read as a number (`-n`), largest first (`-r`). `head -5` keeps the first five. The `|` between two programs is a **pipe**. The kernel, the core of the operating system, connects one program's output to the next program's input, so lines flow from stage to stage with no file in between.

```text
 100759 /v1/authorizations
  59071 /v1/captures
  41915 /healthz
  32574 /v1/refunds
  26302 /v1/tokens
```

Why is the first `sort` there? Because `uniq` compares each line only with the one just before it. It never remembers older lines, so it can only count copies that sit next to each other. Leave the sort out and `/v1/authorizations` shows up on 95,760 separate output lines, most with a count of 1, because other paths keep coming in between. So the job has to bring equal keys together, where a key is the value you group by, here the path. The first sort does that, and that step is the expensive part of every batch job in this track. MapReduce and Spark, the systems that run such jobs on many machines in the next lessons, have it too.

This is a **batch job**: it reads input that already exists and doesn't change while the job runs, and it works out its whole result from scratch each time. If the awk part was wrong, you fix it and run again. The log is untouched, so a bad run costs only time. Let's take the job apart, starting with why it's built from small programs at all.

sections.h: Small programs, one shared format, and the wiring kept outside
sections.body:
None of the five programs in that pipeline knows anything about access logs, or about each other. That's on purpose. Unix is the operating system that Bell Labs, the research lab of the American phone company AT&T, built around 1970, and Linux and macOS follow its ways. Doug McIlroy, who proposed pipes there, wrote the style down in 1978, in a foreword to a special Unix issue of the Bell System Technical Journal. Its first rule is "Make each program do one thing well." The second says to expect every program's output to become the input of another program, one that may not exist yet.

The programs are small. `sort` sorts, `uniq` collapses runs, `head` stops early. Each is easy to test and to trust, and you combine them instead of writing a new program for every question.

They share one format. Every program reads bytes from its standard input and writes bytes to its standard output, the two streams the shell connects for it. By habit, those bytes are lines of text with fields separated by blanks, so any program can feed any other. Change `$7` to `$9` and the same pipeline counts status codes. Change it to `$1` and it counts the computers that sent requests.

And the wiring lives outside them. `awk` doesn't know whether its output goes to a file, a screen or another program; the shell decides. You can add `tee`, a program that saves a copy of whatever passes through it, or swap one stage, without touching the others.

Pipes also run the stages at the same time. Each program runs as its own process, a running program with its own memory. The kernel gives each pipe a small buffer: 64 KiB by default on Linux (a KiB is 1,024 bytes). When the buffer is full, the writer waits until the reader catches up. That's **backpressure**: a slow stage slows the stages before it, instead of filling the memory. When `head` has its lines and exits, the program writing to it gets SIGPIPE on its next write. That's the kernel's notice that nobody is reading any more, and it stops the writer. So `awk '{print $7}' access.log | head -3` returns almost at once.

The figure lines the pipeline up with MapReduce, Google's system for running jobs like this on thousands of machines, which is the next lesson's subject. `awk` is the **map** step: it turns each input record into a key. The first `sort` is the **shuffle**: it brings equal keys together. `uniq -c` is the **reduce** step: it walks each group of equal keys and writes one result. Ranking by count needs a second sort, and in MapReduce that's a second job.

MapReduce kept the small steps, the shared record format (pairs of a key and a value, instead of lines) and the rule that input never changes. It replaced the pipe with files in a distributed file system, one file system spread over many machines' disks, or DFS for short. And it replaced the local sort with a sort across machines. Designing Data-Intensive Applications, a well-known book on these systems, makes the same comparison. A batch system on many machines has the same parts as this one machine: storage behind a file interface, a scheduler that starts programs, and wiring from outputs to inputs. Next, let's look harder at the shuffle, because there's more than one way to bring equal keys together.

aside.title: Why is it called a shuffle if it sorts?
aside.body: The name misleads, as Designing Data-Intensive Applications points out. Shuffling cards mixes them up, while this step does the opposite and leaves equal keys side by side. Think of it as the step that moves every record to where the other records with its key are. On one machine that's a sort. On many machines it's a sort plus a trip across the network, which is why it costs the most.

sections.h: A hash map counts in one pass, until the keys outgrow memory
sections.body:
Sorting isn't the only way to bring equal keys together. The first version of our count doesn't sort at all. It keeps a tally, like the ballot sheet, in a hash map from key to count. A hash map is a table that finds a key's slot in one step. It works out a number from the key, called its hash, and uses that number as the slot's position. Read each line once and add one to its key's count. awk can do it in one line:

```bash
awk '{n[$7]++} END {for (p in n) print n[p], p}' access.log | sort -rn | head -5
```

In Kotlin it's a `HashMap<String, Long>` and `counts.merge(path, 1L, Long::plus)`. Each line costs one hash and one lookup. There's no sort and no disk, and the last `sort` only orders the different paths, not two million lines. This is **hash aggregation**, and while it fits in memory, nothing beats it.

What has to fit? Not the lines: the **distinct keys**, the different values. Counting by endpoint, the eight kinds of request the payments program takes, needs eight entries, a few hundred bytes. Counting raw paths is another matter, because every payment has its own page, such as `/v1/payments/pay_0556303`. The demo log has 351,305 distinct paths, and each one needs an entry that lives until the end of the job.

Kotlin runs on the JVM, the Java virtual machine, the program that runs Kotlin and Java code. There, an entry costs more than its key. It needs the map's entry object, the `String` and the bytes inside it, a `Long` count wrapped in an object of its own, and a slot in the map's table. The demo below measured about 111 bytes per entry for 24-byte paths on Java 25 (JDK 25). So a million distinct paths take about 111 MB of heap, the memory the JVM gives a program's objects. Fifty million idempotency keys, the unique labels apps send with their requests, would take more than 5 GB.

Where it breaks, it breaks all at once. The same demo starts a JVM with a 64 MB heap and keeps adding new paths. It died with `OutOfMemoryError`, the JVM's error for a full heap, after about 617,000 of them. It doesn't slow down gently first. A real job spends its last minutes in garbage collection, the JVM's hunt for memory it can free. Then it dies, usually near the end, after most of the work is done. Reading more slowly doesn't help either, because the map has to hold every distinct key until the last line.

That's the ballot sheet again: fine with five candidates, hopeless with every library card in town. A job tested on a day's sample holds a few hundred thousand keys; a year's input may hold tens of millions. **Count the distinct keys, not the lines. Then choose.** Distinct keys times bytes per entry is the memory the map needs. Counts by endpoint, status, shop or currency almost always fit. Counts by card number, idempotency key or raw path may not. Next, we'll see why sorting escapes this, even though it looks as if it shouldn't.

sections.h: Sorting more than fits in memory: external merge sort
sections.body:
Sorting seems to have the same problem. To put keys in order, surely you need them all in memory at once? A sort done in memory does, and it would fail exactly like the hash map. The trick is never to sort everything at once.

Back at the ballot table, picture a pile too big for the table. Take an armful, sort it by name and set the sorted stack aside, until the pile is gone. Then merge the stacks: look at the top ballot of each, take the one that comes first in the alphabet, and repeat. Equal names come out side by side, and you count them as they pass.

That's an **external merge sort**, the second version of our count. A computer does it in two phases, and the stepper below runs them on twelve keys.

1. Making runs. Read as many lines as fit in a buffer of M bytes, sort them in memory, and write them to a temporary file. That sorted file is a **run**. Repeat until the input ends. N bytes of input give about N / M runs.
2. Merging. Open several runs at once and keep the first line of each in a priority queue, a structure that always hands back its smallest item first. Write the smallest line, read the next line from the run it came from, and repeat. This needs one line, or one read buffer, per open run, however long the runs are. The number of runs one merge reads at once is the **fan-in**, F. With more than F runs, merge them in groups, then merge the results. Each round over all the data is a pass, and each pass turns r runs into r / F, rounded up.

Let's put numbers on it. 100 GB of keys with a 1 GB buffer gives 100 runs. With a fan-in of 16, the first pass leaves 7 runs and the second leaves 1: two merge passes. With a fan-in of 128, one. Each pass reads and writes all 100 GB, but in order, from the start of each file to its end, which disks do fastest. Then `uniq -c` counts the sorted keys with one counter. So sorting costs more processor work and extra trips over the disk, and in exchange it never runs out of memory. It only gets slower as the input grows.

GNU sort, the `sort` on Linux, does all of this without being asked. Its options, from its manual:

| Option | What it sets | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `-S` | the buffer for making runs (also as a % of memory) | chosen by sort |
| `-T` | where runs go (several `-T` spread them over disks) | `$TMPDIR` or `/tmp` |
| `--batch-size` | the fan-in | 16, minimum 2 |
| `--parallel` | threads for the sorting in memory | the number of cores, at most 8 |
| `--compress-program` | a program that compresses runs | none |

Set `LC_ALL=C` too. A locale is a set of language rules, such as where accented letters go in alphabetical order, and `LC_ALL=C` switches them off, so `sort` compares plain byte values. The manual recommends it for the traditional order. On this log it also made `sort` about five times faster than the box's usual locale, a UTF-8 one (UTF-8 is the common way to store text as bytes).

In the Try it, `sort -S 4M` on 46 MB of paths wrote 73 runs. One merge can't read 73 runs at a fan-in of 16, so sort first merged 64 of them in four groups. Then it merged those four results and the 9 runs left over straight into the output: 77 temporary files. It never held more than about 7 MB. The simple model in the stepper and the lab does a little more work: its full passes would have rewritten all 73 runs once more. Either way, one machine can sort far more than its memory. So was one machine ever the problem? Next, we'll see a famous answer.

try.title: Count GNU sort's runs
steps: In the lab box, pull the paths out into a file, then sort it with a 4 MB buffer three times, with fan-ins of 16, 64 and 2. `strace` logs the requests a program makes to the kernel, here every file `sort` opens, and `grep` counts the temporary files it created.
Before you run it: with 73 runs, predict which fan-in creates the most temporary files, and roughly how many.
Then compare the memory `sort` uses with a 4 MB buffer and with its default buffer. `/usr/bin/time -f` prints the most memory a program held, and how long it ran.

code.title: in the lab box
code.src:
cd /tmp
awk '{print $7}' /labs/sim/build/l02/access.log > paths.txt    # 2,000,000 keys, 46 MB
wc -lc paths.txt
export LC_ALL=C
mkdir -p runs
for b in 16 64 2; do
  strace -f -qq -e trace=openat -o trace.txt sort -S 4M --batch-size=$b -T /tmp/runs paths.txt > sorted.txt
  echo "batch-size $b: $(grep -c 'runs/sort.*O_CREAT' trace.txt) temporary files"
done
/usr/bin/time -f '%M KB max memory, %e s' sort -S 4M -T /tmp/runs paths.txt > /dev/null
/usr/bin/time -f '%M KB max memory, %e s' sort -T /tmp/runs paths.txt > /dev/null

try.expect:
```text
 2000000 46478507 paths.txt
batch-size 16: 77 temporary files
batch-size 64: 74 temporary files
batch-size 2: 144 temporary files
6836 KB max memory, 0.72 s
300564 KB max memory, 0.39 s
```

The three counts fit 73 runs. With a fan-in of 64, sort merged 64 runs into one file and then merged that file with the other 9 into the output: 73 + 1. With 16 it needed four merges along the way: 73 + 4. With 2 it merged pairs again and again: 73 + 71. With 4 MB, `sort` stayed under 7 MB of memory. Left to choose its own buffer, it took 300 MB, wrote no temporary files at all and finished sooner. Times vary from run to run; on this laptop they moved by about 50%.

sections.h: When a laptop beats a cluster, and when it stops
sections.body:
In January 2014, Adam Drake answered a blog post by Tom Hayden. Hayden had counted the results of chess games with Hadoop, a free system that runs jobs like ours on many machines. Hayden's job read 1.75 GB of game records on 7 small `c1.medium` machines, rented through Elastic MapReduce, Amazon's service that rents out a ready-made Hadoop cluster. It took about 26 minutes: about 1.14 MB per second. On his laptop, Drake wrote a shell pipeline of `find`, which lists files, `xargs`, which starts a program for each, and two runs of `mawk`, a fast version of awk. It read 3.46 GB, twice the data, in about 12 seconds: about 270 MB per second. Plain `cat`, which reads the files and does nothing else, ran at 272 MB per second. His pipeline was as fast as the disk could hand over the bytes.

His headline says 235 times faster. That number assumes Hadoop would have needed twice as long for twice the data. The raw comparison is 26 minutes against 12 seconds: about 130 times faster, on twice the input. Quote the raw ratio when you use the example. It's strong enough.

His reasons map onto this lesson. The stages of a pipeline run at the same time, like a small cluster on one machine. His awk kept three counters (wins, losses, draws), hash aggregation with a tiny set of keys, so nothing had to be sorted. `xargs -P4` ran four copies of awk on four cores. And `mawk` was faster than `gawk`, the GNU version, for this job. The cluster, meanwhile, paid for starting the job, scheduling its tasks and moving data it didn't need to move. Growing past one machine, in the Foundations track, made the same point with the COST paper. Compare against one good program on one thread before you assume you need more machines.

Your own pipeline may be held back by something else. In the last Try it below, `cat` reads the cached log at gigabytes per second, while the full pipeline manages about 100 MB per second. It's limited by sorting two million keys, not by the disk. Drake's job never sorted at all. Find the slow stage by timing the pipeline one stage longer at a time, and fix that one.

One machine stops being enough in a few clear cases. The input is bigger than its disks. The job is too slow for its deadline even at disk speed: by the formula from Why big data systems exist, 10 TB at 2 GB/s is 83 minutes. A job that runs for hours has to survive a machine dying halfway. Or many teams need to run jobs over the same data. Then you need this lesson's three parts on many machines: storage spread over them, a scheduler that starts the work near the data, and a sort across machines. The next lesson builds them.

steps: In the lab box, in `/labs/sim/build/l02`, time the pipeline one stage longer at a time: `cat` alone, then `awk`, then `awk` into `sort`, then the same with `LC_ALL=C`, then the whole pipeline.
Predict before you run: which stage takes most of the time, the reading, picking out the field, or the sort?

code.src:
TIMEFORMAT='%R s'

Reading 231 MB took a tenth of a second, because the file was in the page cache, the operating system's copy of recently read files in memory. Picking out the field took half a second. The sort took most of the rest: about 9 seconds in the box's UTF-8 locale and under 2 seconds with `LC_ALL=C`. The whole pipeline with `LC_ALL=C` ran in about 2.4 seconds, roughly 100 MB per second. On a second run every number moved (the laptop was busy with other work), but the order of the stages didn't.

compare.title: The same top five, by hashing and by sorting

a.label: Hash aggregation in awk
a.title: one pass, memory per distinct key
a.src:
awk '{n[$7]++} END {for (p in n) print n[p], p}' access.log \
  | sort -rn | head -5

# the map holds 351,305 paths until END
# 40,480 KB max memory in the lab box

b.label: Sort, then count neighbours
b.title: sorted runs, memory bounded by -S
b.src:
awk '{print $7}' access.log \
  | LC_ALL=C sort -S 4M | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -5

# sort keeps a 4 MB buffer and spills runs to disk
# 6,836 KB max memory for sort -S 4M on these keys

compare.note: Both print the same five lines. The awk version keeps one entry per distinct path in a hash map: `/usr/bin/time` measured 40 MB for 351,305 paths, and it would grow with every new path. The sort version keeps a fixed buffer, writes sorted runs to temporary files and merges them, so its memory stays near the `-S` value however many distinct keys the log holds. `uniq -c` then needs one counter. The last `sort -rn` in both is small: it orders the distinct paths, not the two million lines.

worked.title: Find the payments recorded twice in a bank's file

steps.say: Each day, the bank that moves the money for our shops sends a file of every payment it moved: 80 million lines. Column 4 holds each payment's idempotency key, the unique label our program sent with the request, as a 36-character UUID (a standard random ID). A key that appears twice means a payment was moved twice. Almost every key is distinct. First, estimate the hash map: distinct keys times bytes per entry.

Next, size the sort. The keys alone are about 80 million x 37 bytes (with the newline), about 3 GB. With a 256 MB buffer, making runs gives at least 12 of them. GNU sort's runs come out smaller than its buffer, because the buffer also holds bookkeeping for every line. So count them on a sample with the strace trick from the Try it before you trust the number.
steps.code:
// 2. runs and merge passes, with the lab's mergePasses
val keyBytes = 80_000_000L * 37                    // 2,960,000,000 bytes, about 3 GB
val buffer = 256_000_000L
val runs = ((keyBytes + buffer - 1) / buffer).toInt()   // 12 runs, or more on GNU sort
mergePasses(runs, fanIn = 16)                     // 1: a single merge reads all 12
mergePasses(runs * 6, fanIn = 16)                 // 2: if GNU's runs come out six times smaller

steps.say: Write the job as a pipeline. `cut` picks out column 4; it's a simpler awk for files split by commas. `sort` sorts with a fixed buffer and a scratch disk, and `uniq -d` prints one copy of each key that occurs more than once. `LC_ALL=C` gives byte order and a faster sort.
steps.code:

drill.title: Write the merge from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write a function that merges several sorted lists of strings into one sorted list with a priority queue, holding only one element per list at a time. (Merging k lists at once like this is called a k-way merge.) Then say how many passes a fan-in of 10 needs for 250 runs.

recap: `awk '{print $7}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head` is a whole batch job on one machine: awk maps each line to a key, the first sort brings equal keys together, and `uniq -c` reduces each group to a count.
`uniq` compares a line only with the one before it, so without the sort its counts are wrong, with no warning.
The Unix style (small programs, one text format, wiring kept outside the programs) is what MapReduce copied, with files in a distributed file system in place of pipes.
A hash map counts in one pass and wins while the distinct keys fit in memory. On the JVM an entry costs about 100 bytes plus the key, and past the heap it fails all at once.

An external merge sort writes sorted runs the size of its buffer, about N / M of them, and merges them F at a time. Each pass, a full read and write in order, divides the runs by F. GNU sort does it by itself (`-S`, `-T`, `--batch-size` 16, `--parallel` up to 8; set `LC_ALL=C`).

The limit is the machine itself. A laptop pipeline beat a 7-machine Hadoop cluster by about 130 times on the raw numbers. But one machine stops being enough when the data outgrows its disks or its deadline, or the job must survive a machine failing.
closing:
We started with a tally sheet that worked for five candidates and ran out of table for every library card in town. A hash map is that sheet, and it fails all at once. Sorting in runs and merging them never runs out of room; it only gets slower.

On a Mac or Linux, open a terminal and run `history | awk '{print $2}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -5`. It's this lesson's pipeline, pointed at the commands you type most. Then drop the first `sort` and watch the counts fall apart.

Next, we'll spread the file and the sort over many machines, and find out how a job can lose a machine halfway through and still lose nothing.

quiz.q: A teammate runs `awk '{print $9}' access.log | uniq -c` to count status codes, and reports that 201 appears 1, 2 or 3 times at most. What went wrong?
options: `uniq -c` stops counting at a small number by default
The input wasn't sorted, so `uniq` counted only runs of equal lines that sat next to each other
The log is too big for `uniq`, which needs a hash map
quiz.why: `uniq` compares each line only with the one before it. On unsorted input, every interruption starts a new count, so a code appears on thousands of output lines with small counts. Adding `sort` before `uniq -c` brings equal codes together. `uniq` needs almost no memory and has no limit; that's exactly why it depends on sorted input.

quiz.q: A job counts payments per card over a year: 4 billion lines and 300 million different cards. It runs on a JVM with a 16 GB heap. Which plan fits?
options: A `HashMap<String, Long>`, since 4 billion lines need only 300 million entries
Load the whole year into memory and call `sorted()`
An external merge sort (or splitting the keys by hash into files), followed by a count that reads the result in order
Any of them, because the JVM moves the map to disk when it fills
quiz.why: 300 million entries at roughly 100 bytes plus the key is over 30 GB, about twice the heap. Sorting in memory needs all 4 billion lines at once, which is worse. An external sort holds only its buffer. Splitting the keys by hash into files that each fit lets a hash map count one file at a time. A JVM `HashMap` never moves to disk; it throws `OutOfMemoryError`.

quiz.q: A sort of 400 GB uses a 2 GB buffer and a fan-in of 16. How many merge passes does it need after making the runs?
quiz.why: 400 GB / 2 GB gives 200 runs. One pass merges groups of 16, leaving 200 / 16 = 12.5, rounded up to 13 runs, and a second pass merges those 13 into one: 2 passes. One pass would need a fan-in of at least 200. 200 is the run count, not the pass count, and 8 would be about right for a fan-in of 2.

quiz.q: Adam Drake's laptop pipeline read 3.46 GB in about 12 seconds; the Hadoop job read 1.75 GB in about 26 minutes. What's the raw speed-up, and why is it the one to quote?
options: About 235 times, because that is the published headline
About 2 times, because the laptop read twice the data
About 130 times: 26 minutes against 12 seconds, measured on the jobs as they ran
It can't be compared, because the inputs differ
quiz.why: 1,560 seconds divided by 12 is 130, comparing the two runs as measured. The 235x headline assumes Hadoop would have taken twice as long on twice the data, a fair guess that nobody measured. Quoting the raw number keeps the claim honest, and it's still more than a hundred times.

quiz.q: From Why big data systems exist: a nightly job must sort 6 TB of keys, and one machine's disks stream at 2 GB/s. A sort with one merge pass reads the input, writes the runs, reads them back and writes the output. Leaving out the processor's work, about how long does that take on one machine?
quiz.why: Four full trips over 6 TB move 24 TB. At 2 GB/s that's 12,000 seconds, about 3 hours 20 minutes. 50 minutes counts only one read of the input; the runs must be written and read back too. If the deadline is two hours, this is where one machine stops being enough, or where you must read fewer bytes first.

flashcards.back: `uniq` compares each line only with the line before it, so it can only count copies that are next to each other. Sorting makes equal keys neighbours.

flashcards.front: What does a hash aggregation's memory depend on?
flashcards.back: The number of distinct keys, not the number of lines. On the JVM each entry costs about 100 bytes plus the key.

flashcards.front: What are the two phases of an external merge sort?
flashcards.back: Making runs: sort chunks that fit in the buffer and write each one as a sorted run. Merging: read F runs at once through a priority queue and write one sorted run, repeating until one is left.

flashcards.front: How many merge passes do R runs need with fan-in F?
flashcards.back: Each pass turns r runs into r / F, rounded up, until one is left: ceil(log_F(R)) passes. 100 runs need 2 passes at F = 16 and 1 at F = 128.

flashcards.front: GNU sort's defaults for fan-in and threads?
flashcards.back: `--batch-size` (fan-in) 16, minimum 2. `--parallel` is the number of cores, at most 8. `-S` sets the buffer, `-T` the folder for temporary files.

flashcards.front: What happens to a pipeline when `head` exits early?
flashcards.back: The program writing into the pipe gets SIGPIPE, the kernel's notice that nobody is reading, on its next write and stops, so the rest of the input is never read.

flashcards.front: Drake's laptop against Hadoop, raw numbers?
flashcards.back: 3.46 GB in about 12 s on a laptop against 1.75 GB in about 26 minutes on 7 machines: about 130 times faster raw. The 235x headline scales Hadoop up to the same data.

terms.plain: A job that reads existing input without changing it and works out its whole output from scratch, so a bad run can be run again.
A buffer in the kernel that connects one program's output to the next program's input, with both programs running at the same time.
A slow reader slowing down the writer before it: the writer waits when the pipe's buffer is full.
Grouping or counting with a hash map keyed by the group: one pass, and memory for every distinct key.
The different values of the key in the input. A hash map's memory grows with them, not with the lines.
Sorting data bigger than memory by writing sorted runs to disk and merging them a few at a time.
A sorted temporary file written by one round of an external sort.
How many runs one merge reads at once; GNU sort's `--batch-size`.

explain_back.prompt: A friend's Kotlin `HashMap` count died with `OutOfMemoryError` on a 50 GB log. Yet `sort | uniq -c` can count a 500 GB log on a laptop with 16 GB of memory. Explain both, and say when the `HashMap` is the better choice.
explain_back.answer: The HashMap keeps one entry per distinct key until the last line is read, and on the JVM each entry costs about 100 bytes plus the key. If the 50 GB log has a few hundred million distinct keys, that's tens of GB of heap. So it dies, and it dies late, after doing most of the work. `sort` never holds everything. It reads a buffer's worth of lines, sorts them, writes them to a temporary file as a sorted run, and repeats. Then it merges the runs, reading a handful at a time and keeping only the current line of each in memory. Its memory stays near the buffer size whatever the input size. It just needs disk space for the runs and takes longer, because each merge pass reads and writes the data again. Once sorted, equal keys are neighbours, and `uniq -c` counts them with one counter. The HashMap is the better choice when the distinct keys fit easily in memory, such as counts per endpoint, shop or status. Then it makes one pass, does no sorting and touches no disk.

deeper.body:
Real engines don't choose once between hashing and sorting. They start with a hash map and fall back to something else when it fills. One classic fallback is **hash partitioning**. When the map is full, split the keys by a second hash function into, say, 64 partition files on disk. Each file then holds about a 64th of the distinct keys. Then count one file at a time, each with its own hash map that now fits. Every key lands in exactly one file, so the results of different files never need merging. It costs one extra write and read of the data, like one merge pass. The same trick for joining two tables, matching each record in one with records in the other, is called a Grace hash join.

PostgreSQL, a popular free database program, took this route in version 13. A `HashAggregate` step that outgrows `work_mem`, the memory PostgreSQL allows one step of a query, now writes the groups it can't hold to disk in partitions and finishes them afterwards. Older versions could use far more memory than planned. Spark's hash aggregate falls back the other way. When its map runs out of memory, it sorts what it has, writes it to disk, and finishes with a merge. The hash map is the fast path, and the sort is the safety net.

The map step can also shrink the problem before any of this. Say four copies of `awk` each count a quarter of the file in a small hash map, and a last step adds up the four sets of counts. Then the expensive part only sees a few rows per key per copy. That's MapReduce's combiner, and the next lesson builds it. Designing Data-Intensive Applications, in chapter 11 of its second edition, walks through the same log pipeline and the same choice between hashing and sorting, then follows it onto a cluster.
